title: Nine Women Found Dead Near Johannesburg in Two Months. One Outlet Wrote About the President.
subtitle: The contrast between RT Africa's framing and everyone else's
body_md:
A ninth woman's body was found in the Ekurhuleni area east of Johannesburg on September 17, 2026, bringing the total to nine women discovered in the same district over roughly two months. Police offered a R400,000 reward for information and President Ramaphosa ordered a national-priority investigation. Twelve outlets across eleven countries covered the story. Eleven of them foregrounded the women.

[RT Africa](https://www.rt.com/africa/645812-south-african-president-vows-justice-women-murder/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=RSS) ran: "South Africa's president has ordered an urgent murder probe after eight women were found dead near Johannesburg" — framing the story exclusively through the presidential response, citing one fewer victim than every other outlet, and providing no victim voice, community testimony, or analysis of South Africa's gender-based violence context. Every other outlet — from Qatar's Al Jazeera to Pan-African AfricaNews to Canada's Globe and Mail — foregrounded the women, their communities, or the structural violence that produced the deaths.

[Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/18/this-is-a-war-south-africa-battles-femicide-as-womens-bodies-pile-up?traffic_source=rss) deployed the most explicit framing in the corpus, headlining: "'This is a war': South Africa battles femicide as women's bodies pile up." It was the only outlet to invoke war language and the designation "femicide" simultaneously, adopting an activist register absent from every Western Anglophone outlet. Most Anglophone coverage defaulted to the procedural framing: "possible serial killer." [Sky News UK](https://news.sky.com/story/deaths-of-nine-women-in-south-africa-could-be-linked-to-serial-killer-police-say-13588850) ran "Deaths of nine women in South Africa could be 'linked to serial killer', police say." [Hindustan Times](https://www.hindustan.com/) ran: "A ninth woman's body found in South Africa deepens fears of a possible serial killer." Police had not confirmed the killings are linked; [BBC Africa](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2zgk8k8xvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) and BBC World were the only outlets to explicitly note this procedural caution.

[NPR World](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/18/nx-s1-5973822/south-africa-feels-like-a-prison-for-women-amid-spate-of-femicides) produced the most substantive account, naming victim Elizabeth Moselakgomo and supplying baseline statistics that contextualise the case: "over 100 rapes reported and 15 women killed daily" in South Africa as ordinary, not crisis, figures. NPR also reported the public backlash to police advice: "Police haven't ruled out a serial killer and have warned women to be 'vigilant' and not to walk or run alone. The approach is drawing backlash from women on social media who said the onus should be on the police to protect them, not for them to have to curtail their movements." The argument that police framing places responsibility on potential victims rather than on the state appeared only in NPR's coverage.

[Daily Maverick](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-09-17-fourth-ekurhuleni-murder-victim-identified-ninth-womans-body-found/) (South Africa), the domestic outlet, provided the closest investigative detail: identifying a specific victim — the fourth Ekurhuleni victim — and citing a former SAPS profiler calling for cases to be treated as a serial investigation. The domestic outlet also placed the story inside South Africa's established gender-based violence crisis framework, which the national government declared a national disaster in 2025.

Malaysia's [Malay Mail](https://www.malaymail.com/news/world/2026/09/17/we-cannot-continue-picking-up-bodies-south-africa-probes-ninth-womans-death-in-two-months/235562) provided a police quote absent from other coverage: "We cannot continue picking up bodies." It is a different register than either the procedural serial-killer framing or the structural femicide framing — a statement of institutional exhaustion.

The [Globe and Mail](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/video-discovery-of-nine-womens-bodies-raises-fears-of-serial-killer-in-south/) framing was quiet but pointed: "Community on outskirts of Johannesburg appeals for protection as police investigate killings." The appeal came from the community itself, not the state. The juxtaposition — presidential vow on one side, community appeal on the other — reveals the gap between institutional response and lived experience that NPR's data made numerical. South Africa declared gender-based violence and femicide a national disaster in 2025. NPR reported that "many South Africans say the government has not done enough to keep women and girls safe" despite that declaration. The gap between the policy label and the body count is the story the corpus keeps returning to.

Two country-level silences define what is missing. Nigeria, despite shared sub-Saharan African context and a large South African diaspora, has no outlet in this corpus. Germany, South Africa's largest EU trading partner, is also absent. The international amplification of this story is happening without two voices that would most naturally extend the coverage into different political and economic registers — Nigerian press into African solidarity and German press into trade-and-governance framing.
